title: Dominic and the Smile
premise: Rafael Marchetti, a property surveyor who has spent a decade rationalizing the noises in the old Marchetti house he inherited, is forced to confront them when an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside. The house is a ledger of debts: in 1974, Rafael's grandfather took something from the family that lived beneath it, and the house has been holding the payment ever since — in memories, in people, in Rafael's own missing childhood year. To survive, Rafael must gather the scattered descendants of both families and return what was taken, even though doing so means surrendering his own most cherished false memory and letting the house finally close. In the end, justice comes not from law but from witness: the door opens from the inside at last, the taken are named aloud, and the house lets everyone go except the truth.
about_author: Coral Underhill grew up above a funeral parlor in coastal Maine, where she learned early that houses keep accounts. She writes horror about inheritance, obligation, and the things families agree not to remember.

chapters.title: The Appraisal
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. A routine survey of 14 Alder Lane turns strange when his instruments read the basement as 'occupied' by nothing. He catalogs creaks, cold spots, the smell of turned earth, and writes each one a tidy explanation. Emotional beat: the comfort of denial, and how thin it has grown after ten years.

chapters.title: Sealed From the Inside
chapters.summary: Crew foreman Dee Okafor's POV. The excavation for the new foundation hits a stone door set into bedrock, its bolts thrown from within, hinges fused. Dee finds scratch marks on the inside — long ones, patient. She calls Rafael. Emotional beat: professional unease curdling into dread; the first crack in Rafael's explanations.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. That night the noises stop being ambient and become directional — something pacing him room to room. He finds his childhood photo album with one year torn out: age nine to ten, gone. Emotional beat: grief for a memory he didn't know was stolen; the house announces itself as a creditor.

chapters.title: The Marchetti Ledger
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, intercut with 1974 fragments. In his grandfather's effects he finds a surveyor's journal ending mid-sentence in October 1974, and a receipt of sale for land no county records show existing. Emotional beat: the thrill of investigation giving way to the vertigo of complicity — his name is in the margins.

chapters.title: Dee Breaks Protocol
chapters.summary: Dee's POV. Ordered to pour concrete over the door, her crew refuses; two quit, one dreams of scratching. Dee photographs the door and the photos develop wrong — the bolt always on the outside. Emotional beat: solidarity forming between strangers bound by what they've seen; Rafael stops being alone.

chapters.title: Aunt Vesper Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Rafael visits his great-aunt Vesper, sharp at ninety, who insists the family never owned Alder Lane — then describes its kitchen perfectly. She gives him a name: the Okonkwo family, 'the ones under.' Emotional beat: the horror of contested memory; love and lies sharing a mouth.

chapters.title: The Missing Year
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. Hypnosis-adjacent digging into his own mind surfaces a single image: a small hand passing him something through a gap in stone, and his own voice saying 'I'll keep it safe.' Emotional beat: dawning self-horror — he isn't just heir to the debt; he made a promise he can't recall breaking.

chapters.title: Descendants
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Rafael tracks three Okonkwo descendants: Grace, a lawyer who thinks he's running a land-fraud scam; her brother Peter, who has dreamed of the door since childhood; and cousin Amara, who went missing near Alder Lane in 1998. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance; justice requiring witnesses, not lawyers.

chapters.title: Grace's Terms
chapters.summary: Grace's POV. She audits every document Rafael has and finds the 1974 deed legally perfect and physically impossible — notarized by a man who died in 1971. She agrees to help only to prove fraud. Emotional beat: the law as armor against the uncanny, already cracking.

chapters.title: Amara's Room
chapters.summary: Peter and Rafael's POV. They find a bedroom in the house that appears on no floor plan, wallpapered in 1990s posters, dust undisturbed for decades — but warm. On the pillow, a hair ribbon matching Amara's school photo. Emotional beat: hope weaponized; the house showing them exactly enough to keep them.

chapters.title: The Smile
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The presence finally shows itself: not a figure but a smile, wide and gentle, appearing in mirrors, in the grain of wood, in the dark of the sealed door's keyhole. It is patient, almost kind. Emotional beat: terror transmuted into terrible intimacy — the house doesn't hate them; it needs them.

chapters.title: Vesper's Confession
chapters.summary: Vesper's POV, lucid at last. In 1974 her father bought the land knowing the Okonkwos lived below in a settlement predating the town; when they refused to sell, he had the entrance sealed with them inside, calling it a cellar collapse. The town helped. Everyone knew. Emotional beat: generational guilt laid bare; justice outside the law because the law did the burying.

chapters.title: What Was Taken
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The smile shows him the truth: the taken thing is not treasure but names — the Okonkwo family's names, eaten from records, gravestones, and memory, which is why no one could ever find or mourn them. And one more thing: nine-year-old Rafael was given a name to hold and gave it away instead. Emotional beat: understanding the debt precisely; horror becoming responsibility.

chapters.title: Peter Goes Down Alone
chapters.summary: Peter's POV. Impatient with talk, Peter pries at the door and vanishes through it; the house seals happily behind him. Inside he finds a village frozen mid-evening, lamps lit, tables set, and Amara alive, unaged since 1998, setting another plate. Emotional beat: wonder laced with wrongness — preservation as captivity.

chapters.title: The Negotiation
chapters.summary: Grace and Rafael's POV. The house speaks through Vesper's radio and Dee's level: return the names, spoken by blood, witnessed by strangers, before the excavation collapses the roof of the deep rooms on the solstice — four days. Emotional beat: deadline pressure converting dread into purpose; found family assembling around a task.

chapters.title: Recovering the Names
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The names survive only in fragments: a hymn Grace's grandmother hummed, a carved spoon, Vesper's buried memory, the pattern of scratches on the door's inner face — which Dee realizes spell out the family's names in Igbo. Emotional beat: collective restoration; each descendant carrying a piece none could hold alone.

chapters.title: The Town That Knew
chapters.summary: Grace's POV. She files nothing and instead posts the full 1974 account publicly; old families react with fury, fear, and — from a few — shame and help. An elderly former councilman brings the last document: the order to seal the door, signed by Rafael's grandfather. Emotional beat: justice as exposure; the community forced to witness what it chose not to see.

chapters.title: Solstice Eve
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV. The house begins reclaiming its loans: Dee forgets her daughter's face, Grace loses her own surname mid-signature, Rafael feels his remaining memories thinning like paper. The smile grows warmer, more loving, offering to take just him and keep everyone else whole. Emotional beat: temptation at maximum; the price of refusal made flesh.

chapters.title: The Naming
chapters.summary: All POVs converge. At the door, the descendants speak the recovered names aloud, one by one, while the townspeople who came to watch are made to repeat them. Rafael kneels and returns the name he was given at nine — his own middle name, given to the smallest Okonkwo child, the one whose hand passed him the token. Emotional beat: climax as ceremony; restitution performed, not litigated.

chapters.title: The Door Opens From the Inside
chapters.summary: Peter and Amara's POV. The bolts draw back on their own. The frozen village exhales; the dead and the kept — including Amara, who chooses to stay until the last plate is cleared — pass through into whatever waits, unafraid. The smile, finally at rest, becomes simply a crack of light. Emotional beat: release; grief and gratitude indistinguishable.

chapters.title: Closing the Estate
chapters.summary: Rafael's POV, weeks later. The house stands ordinary, surveyed, sold. Rafael donates the land to a memorial garden bearing the Okonkwo names in stone, keeps nothing, and remembers everything now — including the ugly year. Dee pours the foundation; the instruments read empty. Emotional beat: quiet aftermath; the cost and peace of having paid in full.

chapters.title: What Houses Remember
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Vesper's POV, her last autumn. At the garden's dedication she tells the true story to children who will carry it forward, and for the first time in fifty years sleeps without dreaming of scratching. Final image: a new family moves into 14 Alder Lane, and the house makes only the sounds houses make. Emotional beat: found family enduring beyond the haunting; memory as the only justice that lasts.
